_meta: Three tasks sharing one lock under preemptive priority scheduling, used to show priority inversion -- a high-priority task blocked on a lock held by a low-priority task is indirectly delayed by an unrelated MEDIUM-priority task that preempts the lock-holder -- and how priority inheritance fixes it. A preemptive scheduler always runs the highest-priority runnable task. That is correct until a shared lock enters the picture. If a low-priority task L holds a lock that a high-priority task H needs, H must wait for L to release it -- unavoidable, and bounded by L's critical section. The pathology is a third task: a medium-priority task M that needs no lock. Because M outranks L, the scheduler preempts L to run M, and while M runs, L cannot make progress to release the lock, so H -- which outranks M -- is stuck waiting behind M. A high-priority task has been delayed by a lower-priority one that it has no direct dependency on, for as long as M chooses to run. This is priority inversion, and it famously nearly killed the Mars Pathfinder mission. Priority inheritance fixes it: while L holds a lock that a higher-priority task is waiting for, L temporarily inherits that task's priority, so M can no longer preempt L; L finishes its critical section quickly and releases the lock, and H proceeds. tasks gives each task its priority (higher = more important), arrival time, total work, and whether it needs the shared lock. L holds the lock and is low priority; H is high priority and needs the lock; M is medium priority and needs no lock. tasks is the fixture; H's lock-acquisition time and wait under no-inheritance vs priority-inheritance scheduling are computed by simulation.
